client: I've been having a really hard time since my mom passed away last year from cancer. It's like no matter how much time goes by, I still can't seem to concentrate at work — I'll be in the middle of something and then just... drift off, thinking about her. I'm not even sure talking about it is going to change anything, but I figured I should at least try something because I can't keep going on like this.
therapist: I'm so sorry for the loss of your mom — what you're carrying is profound, and the way grief quietly pulls you away mid-thought at work makes complete sense given how deep that love was. I can hear in your voice a kind of exhausted heaviness, like you've been holding this for a long time while still trying to push through, and it takes real courage to reach out even when part of you wonders if it will help. That doubt is completely understandable, but the fact that you're here tells me something important — a part of you is still reaching for something better, and that's exactly where we can start.
vocal_descriptors: very high pitch, soft-spoken, very rapid speech

client: I appreciate you saying that, but honestly... I'm not sure "courage" is the right word for why I'm here. It felt more like desperation, like I've run out of other options and I don't know what else to do with this weight I'm carrying around. I guess part of me is just scared that talking about it won't actually change anything, that I'll still wake up tomorrow and she'll still be gone.
therapist: What you just said is so honest and important — desperation is its own kind of courage, even if it doesn't feel that way, because you're here reaching out despite genuinely not believing it will help. I notice there's a real ache underneath your words, like you're bracing yourself for disappointment even before we've begun, and that makes sense when grief has already taken so much from you. You're right that talking won't bring her back — but what we can work on together is helping you carry that weight differently, so it doesn't keep pulling you under when you're just trying to get through your day.
vocal_descriptors: very high pitch, moderate volume, moderate-paced speech

client: I hear what you're saying, and part of me wants to believe that's possible, but I honestly don't know what "carrying it differently" even looks like. It's been eight months since my mom died and I still can't get through a grocery run without seeing something she would've liked and just... falling apart in the middle of an aisle. I guess what I'm scared of is that you'll give me some breathing exercise or a worksheet and expect that to somehow make a dent in this.
therapist: That image of falling apart in a grocery aisle over something she would have loved — that's not a problem to be fixed with a worksheet, that's love with nowhere left to go, and I want you to know I hear how real and raw that is. Your voice carries something that sounds like a quiet, guarded exhaustion, like you've been waiting for someone to offer you something small when what you're dealing with is enormous. I'm not here to hand you a breathing exercise and call it healing — I want us to actually understand what's happening in those moments, what your mind is doing when grief catches you off guard, so we can work with it rather than just trying to manage it away.
vocal_descriptors: very high pitch, moderate volume, moderate-paced speech

client: I wasn't expecting you to say it like that, and I don't really know what to do with it right now. It almost made me want to cry, which is annoying because I've been holding it together pretty well today, or at least I thought I was. I guess I'm just... not used to someone not rushing past the hard part to get to the solution.
therapist: The fact that tears are right at the surface even on a day you thought you were holding it together tells me that somewhere underneath, something just felt seen — and that can be both a relief and unsettling at the same time. I notice something tender in the way you're speaking right now, soft and careful, like you're not quite sure if it's safe to let that feeling land. You don't have to do anything with it — you're allowed to just sit with it here, and we can move at whatever pace feels right for you.
vocal_descriptors: very high pitch, soft-spoken, moderate-paced speech

client: Yeah, I think that's... that's actually kind of accurate. There's this part of me that wants to just let it out, but then another part that immediately goes "don't be dramatic, you're fine, other people have real problems." I've spent so long telling myself I'm holding it together that I'm not even sure what "not holding it together" would look like anymore.
therapist: That voice that says "don't be dramatic, you're fine" — that's not the truth about your grief, that's a rule you learned somewhere along the way to keep yourself safe, and it's worth gently questioning whether it's actually been protecting you or just keeping you isolated with the pain. I notice you're speaking quickly and softly right now, like the words are tumbling out before that other part of you can stop them, which tells me this is real and close to the surface. Losing your mom to cancer after watching her go through that — that *is* a real problem, and you are allowed to take up that space completely.
vocal_descriptors: very high pitch, soft-spoken, very rapid speech

client: I didn't expect that to hit me so hard, but I can feel my throat tightening right now. Like, I've been telling myself for months that other people have it worse, that I should just be grateful for the time we had, and hearing you say I'm allowed to take up space... I don't even know what to do with that. Part of me wants to believe it, but another part is already looking for reasons why you're just saying that to make me feel better.
therapist: That tightening in your throat right now is your body telling you something true is happening, and I want you to know I'm not saying you're allowed to take up space to make you feel better — I'm saying it because "other people have it worse" has never once in history made anyone's grief smaller or less real. The way you're speaking right now, fast and high and tight, like the words are racing ahead of the part of you that wants to shut it down, tells me that something in you already knows this permission isn't just something I made up. That thought — "I should just be grateful for the time we had" — is worth looking at together, because gratitude and grief aren't opposites, and you don't have to choose between them.
vocal_descriptors: very high pitch, moderate volume, fast speech

client: I hate that you just said that, because part of me really wanted to keep arguing with you and now I can't. I've been telling myself for months that being sad about losing her feels selfish, like I'm making her death about me, but the way you put it... gratitude and grief not being opposites, that actually landed somewhere. I don't fully trust it yet, but I'm not ready to just dismiss it either.
therapist: The fact that you can't quite dismiss it even though part of you wants to — that's not weakness, that's something honest breaking through, and I want to gently stay with what you said about grief feeling selfish, because that belief has been doing a lot of damage quietly. I can hear in your voice something that sounds like you're right at the edge of something, speaking quickly and softly like you're almost afraid of what might come if you slow down — and you don't have to slow down, but I want you to know it's safe here if you do. Grieving your mom isn't making her death about you — it's proof of what she meant to you, and she deserves to have meant that much.
vocal_descriptors: very high pitch, soft-spoken, very rapid speech

client: I didn't expect that to hit me the way it did. Like, I've been telling myself for months that crying about her is somehow making it about me, and hearing you say it out loud like that... I don't know, it made something in my chest just kind of collapse a little. But I'm also scared, because if I actually let myself slow down and feel it, I don't know if I'll be able to stop.
therapist: That fear of not being able to stop — I hear it in your voice, high and fast like you're holding yourself just above the surface — and I want you to know that fear makes complete sense, because you've been holding this back for eight months and that's an enormous amount of weight. But here's what I've seen to be true: grief isn't a flood that swallows you whole if you let it in — it comes in waves, and you have more capacity to survive those waves than that scared part of you believes right now. That collapse you felt in your chest just now wasn't you falling apart — it was something finally being put down, even just for a moment.
vocal_descriptors: very high pitch, moderate volume, fast speech

client: I want to believe that, I really do, but eight months of keeping it together starts to feel like... who you are, you know? Like if I let the wave come, I don't know who I am on the other side of it. And honestly, part of me is still not convinced that it won't just keep going and going until there's nothing left of me.
therapist: What you just described — not knowing who you are on the other side of the wave — that might actually be the most important thing you've said today, because it tells me the grief isn't the only thing you're afraid of, you're also afraid of losing the version of yourself that survived it. I can hear something very tender and careful in your voice right now, like you're speaking from a high, fragile place, and I want to gently offer this: the person who comes through the wave isn't a diminished version of you, they're someone who finally got to love their mom out loud without apology. You've already survived eight months of carrying this alone — that person doesn't disappear when you grieve, that person is exactly who makes it through.
vocal_descriptors: very high pitch, moderate volume, moderate-paced speech

client: I hear what you're saying, and part of me wants to believe it, but I'm not sure I do yet. Like, the version of me who survived was built on not falling apart, on being the one who kept things moving, and I don't know how to be a person who just... lets herself be sad about her mom without it feeling like a collapse. And honestly, the idea of loving her "out loud without apology" almost makes me more anxious, because what if I start and I can't stop?
therapist: The way you're speaking right now — fast and high and tight, like the words are outrunning something — tells me that anxiety is very real and present, not just an idea. I want to gently challenge one thing though: you've described yourself as "the one who kept things moving," but you've also been quietly falling apart in grocery store aisles for eight months, which means you've already been living inside the wave — you just haven't had anyone standing with you in it yet. Letting yourself be sad about your mom isn't the collapse of who you are; it might actually be the first time who you are gets to be fully honest.
vocal_descriptors: very high pitch, moderate volume, very rapid speech
